terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see tonight's call signs and the weekend rotas compared.

tasks.title: How many teams called in
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `call_signs.py`, write a function called `different_signs` that takes a list of call signs as they were heard, some of them more than once, and gives back how many different call signs there are. For tonight it gives back `4`. Print what it gives back for `heard`.

Check calls `different_signs` with lists of its own, an empty one too, and looks at what it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on what a set is.
Make a set from the list.
Give back how many items the set holds.
Print it for `heard` and compare it with `len(heard)`.
hints: A set holds each value once, however many times it was added.
`set()` makes a set from a list, and `len` tells how many items a set holds.

tasks.title: The first call heard twice
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, write a function called `first_repeat` that takes a list of call signs as they were heard, and gives back the first call sign that is heard for a second time, or `None` when no call sign is heard twice. For tonight it gives back `Bravo two`. Keep the call signs heard so far in a set. Print what it gives back for `heard`.

Check calls `first_repeat` with lists of its own and looks at what it gives back. In one of them, the call sign heard first is not the first to be heard again.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on a set for what you have seen.
Start an empty set before the loop.
For each call sign, ask whether it is in the set already: if so, that is the answer.
If not, add it to the set. After the loop, give back `None`.
hints: Go through the calls in order and remember each one you have heard. The first call you already remember is the answer.
An empty set is made with `set()`, not `{}`. `in` asks whether a value is in it, and `add` puts one in. Ask before you add.
The shape is `seen = set()`, then `for call in calls:` with `if call in seen:` and `return call`, then `seen.add(call)`, and `return None` after the loop.

tasks.title: On both rotas
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, write a function called `on_both` that takes two rotas, two lists of names, and gives back a set of the names that are on both. For Friday and Saturday it gives back a set of `Rhona` and `Kirsty`, in whatever order Python prints it. Print what it gives back for `friday` and `saturday`.

Check calls `on_both` with rotas of its own and looks at what it gives back: a set, compared whatever its order.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on comparing two sets.
Make a set from each rota.
Give back the set of the names that are in both.
Print it, and run the file twice: the order may change, the names do not.
hints: Two sets can be combined in a few ways: what is in either, what is in both, what is in one and not the other.
`&` between two sets gives the items that are in both. It works on sets, so make each list a set first.

videos.title: Sets and what they are for

tasks.title: Call signs we do not know
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, write a function called `unknown_signs` that takes a list of call signs heard and a list of call signs the team knows, and gives back a list of the call signs heard that are not known, each once, in alphabetical order. For tonight it gives back `['Delta four']`. Print what it gives back for `heard` and `known`.

Check calls `unknown_signs` with lists of its own, one with an unknown call sign heard twice, and looks at what it gives back: a list, in alphabetical order.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on comparing two sets and on putting a set in order.
Make a set of what was heard and a set of what is known.
Take away the known ones from the heard ones.
Give back the rest as a list in alphabetical order.
hints: A set has no order, so the order comes at the end, from turning the set into a sorted list.
`-` between two sets gives the items of the first that are not in the second. `sorted` takes a set and gives back a list in order.
